AI.motivation: To explore efficient algebraic frameworks for simulating quantum circuits and leverage computational advantages of hard-core bosons.
AI.method: The paper reviews and extends hard-core boson algebra, implements it for circuit simulation, and compares performance with IBM Qiskit.
AI.result: Significantly improved execution times for simulations compared to traditional methods, with a new application combining hard-core bosons with genetic algorithms for quantum circuit synthesis.
AI.conclusion: The hard-core boson approach is both computationally advantageous and opens new avenues for quantum circuit synthesis.

title: The Role of Scintillation in Detecting HI Absorption in FRB Spectra
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Under review; comments welcome
summary: The 21-cm absorption line of neutral hydrogen has been a long hypothesized observational feature of the spectra of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs). The difficulties associated with detector noise in extracting HI absorption have been previously studied. We test the role that scintillation plays in the HI absorption line's detectability, and characterize the regimes where a realistic FRB may yield the 21-cm line. We build an efficient model to simulate diffractive scintillation arising from FRB passage through a thin scattering screen. We find that the absorption profile is detectable in a scintillation-dominated high signal-to-noise spectrum if the scintillation decorrelation bandwidth differs significantly in scale from the width of the absorption profile. Active repeaters also enable favorable conditions as the absorption signal improves when repeat bursts are stacked. Repeat bursts must be separated in time by more than the diffractive scintillation timescale, otherwise flux modulations with frequency are correlated. By cross-referencing repeating FRB positions with an observational catalog of Milky Way molecular clouds detected in CO, we find that the sightline to FRB 20180916B may intersect a Galactic molecular cloud. For currently operating and planned sensitive telescopes, the presence of both scintillation and noise requires $\gtrsim 1000$ bursts to be stacked to detect the HI absorption line at a $5σ$ significance. Improvement in detector sensitivities will help probe HI clouds intersected by FRBs in the host or intervening galaxies, or in high-redshift minihalos.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the detectability of the 21-cm HI absorption line in Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), demonstrating that scintillation has a significant role in this detectability.
AI.motivation: Understanding the 21-cm absorption line in FRBs could provide insights into the interstellar medium and the evolution of galaxies.
AI.method: The authors developed a model to simulate scintillation effects on the HI absorption line during FRB passage through a thin scattering screen, focusing on conditions for detectability and noise levels.
AI.result: They found the absorption profile can be detected in high signal-to-noise conditions when scintillation characteristics differ from the absorption width and noted improved conditions for active repeaters when stacking burst signals.
AI.conclusion: Approximately 1000 burst signals need to be stacked to detect the HI absorption line reliably, and improved telescope sensitivity is essential for probing HI clouds in various astronomical contexts.

title: Squeezing enhanced homodyne weak force sensing in cavity optomechanics
summary: Cavity optomechanical systems have emerged as a promising platform for quantum sensing. Quantum mechanics imposes a standard quantum limit (SQL) on the force-sensitivity for the standard homodyne phase quadrature measurement of the cavity's output field. In this paper, we investigate ways to enhance sensitivity beyond SQL for weak-force measurement by adopting a variational homodyne quadrature readout and quantum squeezing. Our study reveals a remarkable improvement in the force sensitivity of a cavity optomechanical sensor at a suitable homodyne angle, compared with standard phase quadrature detection of the cavity output field within a specific frequency band. We show that the force sensitivity can be further improved by intra-cavity squeezing (ICS) or injected external squeezing (IES) of the cavity mode. Both variational homodyne readout and quantum squeezing induce quantum correlation between the amplitude and phase quadratures of the cavity's output field, thereby improving the force sensitivity. The squeezing-enhanced variational homodyne detection scheme can enable high-precision sensing across various hybrid quantum platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper explores enhancing force sensitivity in cavity optomechanical systems beyond the standard quantum limit using variational homodyne readout and quantum squeezing techniques.
AI.motivation: To surpass the standard quantum limit in weak-force measurements within cavity optomechanical systems, improving their efficacy as quantum sensors.
AI.method: The authors employed a variational homodyne quadrature readout technique and tested intra-cavity and external squeezing to achieve enhanced force sensitivity.
AI.result: The study demonstrated significant improvements in force sensitivity at specific homodyne angles, benefiting from both variational readout and quantum squeezing techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational homodyne detection scheme, bolstered by squeezing, offers a path toward high-precision sensing across diverse quantum platforms.

title: Continuation of Force-Free Electrodynamics upon the loss of magnetic dominance
comment: 31 pages, 5 figures, a supplemental movie for Fig. 3 is available (see ancillary file or https://youtu.be/W8cHlx0qxf0)
summary: Force-Free Electrodynamics (FFE) describes the evolution of the electromagnetic field in magnetically dominated plasmas, but ceases to be hyperbolic once the magnetic dominance condition $F^{ab}F_{ab}>0$ is lost. We demonstrate that, after the loss of magnetic dominance, FFE may be replaced by a theory of null fields, $F^{ab}F_{ab}=0=F^{ab}\tilde{F}_{ab}$, characterized by the condition that its principal null direction is tangent to a geodesic congruence. In flat spacetime, this theory may be equivalently stated as the condition that the field satisfies $\vec{B}^2-\vec{E}^2=0=\vec{E}\cdot\vec{B}$ and the integral curves of the drift velocity $\vec{E}\times\vec{B}/\vec{B}^{2}$ are straight lines. We develop the general structure and the properties of this theory and test it against 1D PIC simulations using the collision of planar symmetric Alfvén waves. We find that the force-free combined with the null continuation shows remarkable macroscopic agreement with PIC simulations, including the birth and evolution of the null region ($F^{ab}F_{ab}=0$) and the formation of a current sheet. As an independent test, we apply the null continuation to Adhikari's type-changing solution, an exact FFE solution exhibiting finite-time loss of magnetic dominance, and also find macroscopic agreement with 1D PIC simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a theory of null fields that replaces Force-Free Electrodynamics (FFE) after magnetic dominance is lost, demonstrating its properties and success in matching PIC simulations.
AI.motivation: To address the breakdown of hyperbolicity in FFE when magnetic dominance is lost and to provide a viable theoretical alternative.
AI.method: The authors propose a null fields theory characterized by specific conditions on electromagnetic fields and validate it using one-dimensional Particle-in-Cell (PIC) simulations of Alfvén wave collisions and a type-changing solution.
AI.result: The null fields theory shows macroscopic agreement with PIC simulations, accurately capturing the dynamics of the null region and current sheet formation following the loss of magnetic dominance.
AI.conclusion: The combined approach of FFE and null continuation effectively models plasmas in conditions where magnetic dominance is lost, providing a consistent framework for understanding their dynamics.

title: Static features from mixing in short- and long-range Lindbladians: Markov property and correlations
summary: The classification of mixed-state phases requires criteria beyond two-point correlation functions, such as the decay of the mutual information (MI) and the conditional mutual information (CMI), with the latter encapsulated in the notion of Markov length. Here we show how such static properties of the fixed point of a Lindbladian follow from natural dynamical features of its generators: rapid mixing and frustration-freeness. We focus on systems with long-range interactions, and prove (i) that local Lindbladians satisfying (global) rapid mixing and frustration-freeness have fixed-points whose CMI decays with the shielding distance, and (ii) that (local) rapid mixing together with primitivity and regularity implies global decay of MI. For long-range interactions decaying with a power law with rate $α$, both quantities decay polynomially rather than exponentially, in contrast to the finite- and short-range regimes where exponential decay (a finite Markov length) is expected within a phase. We further show that Gibbs states of long-range, non-commuting Hamiltonians satisfy a local Markov property at any temperatures, extending the recent results (Chen--Rouzé, 2025) for short-range systems to the long-range regime relevant to a variety of experimental platforms. As a numerical example, we study the long-range Ising model both with and without a transverse field. We find regimes in which the polynomial decay of the CMI holds, in accordance with the bounds proven.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the classification of mixed-state phases, emphasizing the importance of mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI) while analyzing the dynamical features of Lindbladian generators, particularly in long-range interacting systems.
AI.motivation: To enhance the classification of mixed-state phases beyond traditional two-point correlations by incorporating criteria like mutual information decay and Markov properties.
AI.method: The paper proves that local Lindbladians with rapid mixing and frustration-freeness exhibit fixed points with specific decay properties for CMI and MI, particularly in long-range interactions, showing polynomial rather than exponential decay.
AI.result: It is demonstrated that within long-range interacting systems, local conditions lead to polynomial decay of CMI and MI, with verified examples from the long-range Ising model confirming these findings.
AI.conclusion: The findings extend known results for short-range systems to long-range Hamiltonians and provide insight into the static properties dictated by dynamic features, posing implications for various experimental platforms.

title: Single Electrons in a Dual-Plane Printed-Circuit-Board Penning Trap
comment: 10 pages, 8 figures, submitted to Phys. Rev. Applied
summary: We demonstrate single-electron trapping and detection in a two-dimensionally scalable dual-plane printed-circuit-board Penning trap. We characterize deterministic electron loading, axial damping, axial temperature, and collision-induced magnetron-radius growth at low magnetic fields. These results establish a practical platform for planar Penning traps and identify key next steps toward applications in quantum information science.

AI.tldr: The study presents a scalable dual-plane printed-circuit-board Penning trap that enables efficient single-electron trapping and detection.
AI.motivation: To develop a practical platform for planar Penning traps that can be utilized in quantum information science.
AI.method: Characterization of electron loading, axial damping, temperature, and magnetron-radius growth in low magnetic fields using a dual-plane design.
AI.result: Demonstrated efficient single-electron trapping and provided detailed characterization of several key parameters influencing trap performance.
AI.conclusion: The findings pave the way for future applications in quantum information, emphasizing the next steps for enhancing planar Penning traps.

title: A Reproducible Pipeline for Symmetry-Respecting Excited States on Near-Term Quantum Computers: The H2O/STO-3G Case
summary: Variational excited-state quantum algorithms fail for reasons usually studied in isolation: barren plateaus, symmetry contamination, finite-sampling instability, and hardware cost. Using one small but complete system -- H$_2$O in the STO-3G basis (12 qubits, Jordan--Wigner) -- we assemble these into a single reproducible pipeline, checking every claim against exact diagonalization. The bare qubit Hamiltonian interleaves cation ($N{=}7$) states below the neutral manifold; hardware-efficient and number-conserving ansätze stall at Hartree--Fock, an exact stationary point by Brillouin's theorem, while ADAPT-VQE escapes; variational deflation inherits the contamination and inverts the spectrum, whereas the quantum equation-of-motion (qEOM) subspace method restores the ladder to sub-milli-Hartree accuracy. Particle number is protected \emph{structurally} under shot noise, and a realistic measurement model collapses the thousands of subspace matrix elements to $\sim\!10^5$ commuting groups; a matrix-aware shot allocation then reaches chemical accuracy at $\sim\!3\times10^9$ total shots -- a thousandfold below the naive per-element estimate and reachable in days -- leaving single-circuit gate fidelity, not measurement, as the binding constraint. This work is a teaching and benchmarking reference, not a new method; all code, parameters, and figures are released.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes variational excited-state quantum algorithms, focusing on their failures due to several factors, and proposes an effective pipeline using H$_2$O as a case study.
AI.motivation: To address the collective challenges faced by variational excited-state quantum algorithms.
AI.method: Assembled a comprehensive pipeline evaluating multiple failure modes (barren plateaus, symmetry contamination, etc.) using H$_2$O, validated against exact diagonalization, and applied various methods including ADAPT-VQE and qEOM.
AI.result: Demonstrated that while traditional ansätze stall, qEOM restores accuracy; achieved chemical accuracy in computational resources significantly lower than conventional estimates, with single-circuit fidelity as the main limiting factor.
AI.conclusion: Provided a reproducible framework that serves as a reference for teaching and benchmarking, with all supporting materials made publicly available.

title: Optimizing Resource Costs: A Practical Guide to Achieving Target Security in Verifiable Blind Quantum Computing
summary: Verifiable blind quantum computing (VBQC) enables a resource-limited client to securely delegate computations to an untrusted quantum server while maintaining privacy and detecting deviations from the prescribed computation. The noise-robust VBQC protocol of Leichtle et al. achieves this through a round-based structure: the client delegates multiple computation rounds and test rounds, using the test outcomes to detect cheating while tolerating honest hardware noise. The protocol's security proof involves numerous interdependent parameters, making it non-trivial to find a valid parameter set for a given hardware noise level and security target. We formalize this as a constrained optimization problem and develop a practical framework to solve it. The framework yields the protocol parameters that minimize the number of rounds for any given setup. We derive a heuristic formula for the minimal number of rounds to help understand the scaling with noise and security targets and to provide rapid resource estimation. Since the number of rounds depends on noise while the time per round depends on hardware rate, the framework also enables optimization of rate-fidelity trade-offs to minimize end-to-end runtime. We demonstrate both applications through a case study of a trapped-ion server with a measurement-only client, showing how the client's polarization control hardware specifications translate into protocol parameters and runtime estimates, providing concrete guidance for near-term implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a framework for optimizing parameters in verifiable blind quantum computing (VBQC) to minimize computational rounds while ensuring security against untrusted servers and managing hardware noise.
AI.motivation: To enable resource-limited clients to securely delegate quantum computations to untrusted servers, while maintaining privacy and ensuring the ability to detect cheating amidst hardware noise.
AI.method: Formalizing parameter selection as a constrained optimization problem, the authors develop a framework that minimizes rounds in the VBQC protocol based on hardware noise and security levels. They also create a heuristic formula to quickly estimate resources.
AI.result: The framework successfully identifies optimal protocol parameters and demonstrates applications with a trapped-ion server and measurement-only client, linking hardware specifications to runtime estimates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework allows for effective optimization of VBQC, balancing noise resilience and security requirements, providing practical guidance for future implementations.

title: Time Evolution on Hybrid Tensor Networks -- A Novel and Parallelizable Algorithm
summary: We develop a novel time-evolution algorithm for matrix product states based on the recently introduced hybrid tensor network (hTN) framework. We retain the tensors close to the boundary on the classical computer and offload the highly entangled inner ones to the quantum computer. In our variant, we employ the Basis Update and Galerkin (BUG) integrator to time-evolve the classical tensors, and we develop a coupling scheme between the classical and quantum parts. Our framework admits modular combination with any quantum time-evolution method, such as (classically pre-optimized) Trotterization. The ratio of classical and quantum tensor degrees of freedom can be dynamically adjusted during the time evolution, which can be advantageous when the classical memory requirements become prohibitive. The quantum and classical components can run in parallel during a single time step and are not constrained by synchronization barriers or mid-circuit measurements. We describe the detailed steps and pseudocode for our algorithm specialized for tensor networks originating from the matrix product state Ansatz.

AI.tldr: A new algorithm for time-evolving matrix product states using a hybrid tensor network framework allows dynamic balancing of classical and quantum tensor loads, facilitating parallel processing without synchronization issues.
AI.motivation: To improve efficiency in simulating quantum systems by leveraging both classical and quantum computing capabilities in a modular fashion.
AI.method: The algorithm employs the Basis Update and Galerkin (BUG) integrator for classical tensor evolution while offloading inner entangled tensors to a quantum computer, enabling flexible resource allocation.
AI.result: The method allows for dynamic adjustment of classical and quantum components during time evolution and supports parallel execution at each time step without synchronization constraints.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enhances the simulation of matrix product states by integrating classical and quantum computations effectively, providing a robust solution for managing resources in quantum algorithms.

title: Vacuum Fluctuation-Induced State Switching in Degenerate Optical Parametric Oscillators
summary: Bistable driven-dissipative systems near bifurcations can exhibit noise-activated switching between steady states. Here, we investigate how quantum vacuum fluctuations induce such switching in a biased optical parametric oscillator (OPO), a nonlinear system with intrinsic bistability. We show how microscopic quantum fluctuations driving macroscopic transitions can be controlled with an external bias field that reshapes the OPO steady-state metapotential. We derive analytical expressions for the average switching time and validate them through simulations of the OPO field distribution and inter-state probability flow under bias injection. We further examine how switching depends on bias strength, pump gain, and optical nonlinearity. Our findings clarify how quantum noise can shape macroscopic dynamics and provide a foundation for noise-assisted photonic machine learning and probabilistic quantum gates.

AI.tldr: This study explores how quantum vacuum fluctuations influence noise-activated switching in a biased optical parametric oscillator, demonstrating control over microscopic fluctuations and their impact on macroscopic transitions, complemented by analytical expressions and simulations.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of quantum vacuum fluctuations in noise-activated switching in bistable systems, particularly focusing on optical parametric oscillators.
AI.method: The authors derive analytical expressions for average switching time and perform simulations to study the OPO field distribution and inter-state probability flow under varying bias conditions.
AI.result: They establish relationships that reveal how switching dynamics are affected by bias strength, pump gain, and optical nonlinearity, validated through simulations and analytical calculations.
AI.conclusion: The research enhances understanding of quantum noise in macroscopic dynamics and lays groundwork for applications in photonic machine learning and probabilistic quantum computing.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sample-efficient recognition of topological phases
summary: With increasing maturity of quantum computers, standard methods for characterizing global properties of their output quantum states via direct measurements and classical post-processing are becoming increasingly impractical due to large measurement costs. Although quantum neural networks could directly process quantum states to identify underlying characteristics with reduced measurement efforts, they often require deep quantum circuits that cannot be implemented on existing devices. To overcome these challenges, we introduce a hybrid quantum-classical neural network that consists of a shallow parameterized quantum circuit, measurements, and a classical neural network. The parameterized quantum circuit performs a nonlocal transformation of the measurement basis, which is jointly trained with the classical neural network to maximize the statistical distance between data obtained by measuring different quantum states. Using supervised learning, we demonstrate that the hybrid neural network distinguishes the topological phase of the surface code from a symmetry-enriched topological phase and random product states. Moreover, this hybrid neural network reduces both inference and training sample complexities of recognizing the topological phase by approximately one order of magnitude compared to a classical neural network trained on randomized Pauli measurements. As this hybrid neural network features a shallow quantum circuit that can be readily implemented on existing quantum computers, it enables the efficient characterization of complex quantum states.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical neural network to efficiently characterize quantum states using a shallow quantum circuit, significantly reducing measurement and training complexities.
AI.motivation: To address the impractical measurement costs in characterizing quantum states with increasing quantum computer capabilities.
AI.method: A hybrid network combines a shallow parameterized quantum circuit with a classical neural network, jointly trained to enhance statistical distance in measurements of different quantum states.
AI.result: It successfully distinguishes topological phases and reduces inference and training complexities by roughly an order of magnitude compared to classical methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid neural network enables effective characterization of complex quantum states using a readily implementable shallow quantum circuit.

title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for Recognizing Quantum Phases
summary: Identifying quantum phases of matter is key to understanding strongly correlated materials, but remains a challenging task for both conventional computers and current quantum processors. Here, we introduce and implement a hybrid quantum-classical neural network for quantum phase recognition by combining a hardware-efficient parameterized quantum circuit and a feedforward neural network. We jointly train both components with superconducting quantum hardware in the optimization loop, to experimentally demonstrate a classifier for the quantum phases of surface code lattices with up to 4x4 sites in a magnetic field. To learn nonlocal features of the topological phase, we train the hybrid neural network to distinguish topological ground states of the surface code from a featureless ensemble of product states. This allows the trained classifier to distinguish topological ground states from randomly chosen product states, even when subjected to any single-qubit Pauli error. The classifier reaches accuracies above 85% in single-shot measurements, and above 99% when averaging over ten measurements. We expect hybrid neural networks such as the one presented here to be a promising approach for characterizing quantum states in scenarios where classical methods exhibit an unfavorable scaling of sample complexity.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical neural network is introduced for recognizing quantum phases, demonstrating high accuracy in distinguishing topological ground states from product states, with practical applications using superconducting quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Identifying quantum phases in strongly correlated materials is crucial but challenging for classical and quantum methods.
AI.method: A hybrid architecture merges a parameterized quantum circuit with a feedforward neural network, jointly trained using superconducting hardware to classify quantum phases in surface code lattices.
AI.result: The classifier achieves over 85% accuracy in single-shot measurements and over 99% with averaging across ten measurements when distinguishing topological ground states from product states, even under Pauli errors.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid neural networks show promise for efficiently characterizing quantum states, outperforming classical methods in scaling sample complexity.

title: Noise-Directed Adaptive Remapping for Integer Optimization: from qubits to (encoded) qudits
summary: We extend Noise-Directed Adaptive Remapping (NDAR), a recently proposed heuristic meta-algorithm that leverages device noise as a computational resource, to optimization problems over discrete (integer) domains. While originally introduced for unconstrained binary optimization, the proposed generalization introduces additional gauge degrees of freedom at the logical level, such that the gauge transformation applied at each iteration is no longer unique, allowing tailoring to particular encodings or quantum hardware. We identify encoding-dependent requirements for NDAR beyond binary domains: feasibility of the noise attractor, existence of compatible gauge transformations that preserve an efficiently implementable circuit family, and a systematic way to select the transform to apply at each step. We analyze these criteria for qudit-native and for binary, one-hot, and domain-wall qubit encodings, using the Max-k-colorable subgraph problem as a running example. We demonstrate that these encodings can exhibit distinct advantages and tradeoffs when integrated within the NDAR framework, particularly in how noise-induced dynamics interact with the solution landscape and choice of encoding. Our results indicate that NDAR-guided noise considerations provide a new criterion for comparing device-level encoding choices for quantum optimization. Finally, we outline directions toward experimental realization in superconducting qudit devices and further algorithmic improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Noise-Directed Adaptive Remapping (NDAR) for discrete optimization, introducing gauge degrees of freedom for tailored encodings on quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: To optimize problems over discrete domains using device noise as a computational resource, improving upon binary optimization.
AI.method: A generalization of NDAR with encoding-dependent requirements for gauge transformations, analyzed through various encoding methods on the Max-k-colorable subgraph problem.
AI.result: Different encoding schemes (qudit-native, binary, etc.) show varying advantages in noise dynamics and solution landscapes within the NDAR framework.
AI.conclusion: NDAR offers a new criterion for comparing encoding choices in quantum optimization, suggesting pathways for experimental realization and algorithmic enhancements.

title: Parameter-Efficient Continuous-Variable Photonic Quantum Neural Networks for Edge Quantum AI: Demonstration in Oral Cancer Detection
summary: Early detection of oral cancer markedly improves clinical outcomes, yet specialized diagnostic tools remain scarce in low-resource settings. Smartphone-based screening is a scalable alternative but needs lightweight models that run within edge-hardware constraints. Hybrid classical-quantum architectures are emerging candidates for parameter-efficient learning, yet most rely on qubit hardware that needs cryogenic operation, unsuitable for edge deployment. Continuous-variable (CV) photonic quantum computing, which operates at room temperature, offers a complementary route. We investigate a hybrid classical-CV quantum classifier for oral cancer detection from smartphone images. The pipeline combines a MobileNetV1 feature extractor, principal component analysis to 16 dimensions, and a parameterized CV-QNN of displacement, interferometric, and Kerr gates on a photonic backend. We propose a simplified $Φ\circ D \circ U_1$ CV-QNN architecture that cuts trainable parameters 40-45% relative to the standard CV-QNN layer of Killoran et al. (2019a), and identify dimensionality-reduction and encoding-restriction strategies that mitigate barren plateaus, raising loss-gradient variance by roughly 58 orders of magnitude. Whether the simplified layer beats the full layer is width-dependent: the full layer holds a small but significant edge at two qumodes, whereas the simplified layer is significantly better at four qumodes using 44% fewer parameters. The strongest model, a four-qumode simplified CV-QNN with only 18 parameters, attains the highest validation AUC of all models, exceeds a 55-parameter classical baseline using 67% fewer parameters, and reaches 100% calibrated test accuracy across all seeds. These results support CV photonic quantum machine learning for parameter-efficient, room-temperature medical image classification and motivate progress toward edge quantum AI.

AI.tldr: A hybrid classical-CV quantum classifier for early oral cancer detection using smartphone images shows advantages in parameter efficiency and accuracy over classical models.
AI.motivation: Early oral cancer detection can improve outcomes, but low-resource settings lack necessary diagnostic tools; thus, there's a need for efficient, scalable alternatives like smartphone-based screening.
AI.method: The paper proposes a pipeline combining MobileNetV1 feature extraction, dimensionality reduction via PCA, and a CV-QNN comprising simplified CV-QNN architectures that are less resource-intensive and effective at room temperature.
AI.result: The proposed simplified model performs better under certain conditions than full CV-QNN models, achieving significant accuracy with fewer parameters, and displaying a 100% calibrated test accuracy across various seeds.
AI.conclusion: The findings advocate for the use of CV photonic quantum technology in efficient, room-temperature medical image classification, promoting advancements in edge quantum AI solutions for healthcare.

title: Efficient targeting of arbitrary excited states with quantum inverse power iteration through filtering polynomials
summary: In this work, we introduce a quantum inverse power iteration (QIPI) algorithm based on the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) to target arbitrary excited states. Given an energy shift $ω$, QIPI prepares the target excited state by iteratively applying an approximation of the shifted inverse Hamiltonian $(H-ωI)^{-1}$ to a trial state. Prior quantum inverse power approaches typically relied on Fourier decompositions of the inverse Hamiltonian, with numerical quadrature used to reconstruct the transformation, but such methods are highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and have been observed to be numerically unstable, effectively restricting their use to ground-state preparation. To enable robust excited-state targeting, we investigate two alternative transformation techniques: a Chebyshev decomposition of the inverse (Cheb-inv) and an eigenstate filtering (EF) approach based on QSVT. We find that EF-based QIPI is substantially more robust than Cheb-inv and other decomposition-based approaches due to the symmetry of the applied filtering polynomial, avoiding divergence with respect to the choice of $ω$ and efficiently suppressing off-target eigenstates even in closely spaced spectra. Numerical simulations for molecular Hamiltonians of H$_2$, LiH, and BeH$_2$ show improved convergence and enhanced access to higher excited states relative to other quantum power methods. Assuming standard oracle access to the Hamiltonian, we further provide logical resource estimates in fault-tolerant settings in terms of T gate counts, and conclude that QIPI can achieve high target state amplification with modest polynomial degrees, thereby making it a promising candidate for scalable excited-state preparation in fault-tolerant quantum chemistry applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a quantum inverse power iteration (QIPI) algorithm for preparing excited states using quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), introducing alternative methods to enhance robustness and stability compared to previous approaches.
AI.motivation: The need for stable and efficient methods to prepare excited states in quantum systems, addressing the limitations of traditional inverse power methods that struggle with numerical instability and hyperparameter sensitivity.
AI.method: QIPI leverages Chebyshev decomposition and eigenstate filtering (EF) techniques within the framework of QSVT, iteratively applying an approximate shifted inverse Hamiltonian to a trial state.
AI.result: EF-based QIPI demonstrates improved robustness and efficiency in targeting excited states, showing better convergence in numerical simulations of molecular Hamiltonians compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: QIPI is a promising method for scalable excited-state preparation in quantum chemistry, offering high target state amplification with manageable resource requirements in fault-tolerant quantum settings.

title: Efficient Approximation of the Wigner Kernel in Phase-Space Quantum Mechanics
comment: Preprint of the manuscript submitted to the Applied Mathematical Modelling Journal of Elsevier
summary: The Signed Particle Formulation provides a particle-based interpretation of quantum mechanics in phase space, where quantum dynamics are represented through the creation and evolution of signed particles. A central computational challenge in this framework is the evaluation of the Wigner kernel, which generally involves highly oscillatory integrals and can become computationally demanding in time-dependent simulations. This paper proposes an analytical approximation of the Wigner kernel for one-dimensional single body quantum systems by exploiting a series-based representation of the potential function. The resulting expression provides an efficient way to approximate the Wigner kernel and the associated Gamma function, which governs the particle-generation process in the Signed Particle Formulation framework. The proposed approximation is evaluated for several Gaussian-based potential profiles, including single, double, triple, and quadruple Gaussian potentials. Numerical comparisons between the approximated and directly computed Wigner kernels and Gamma functions show that the proposed method captures the main behavior of the exact quantities while significantly reducing the computational cost. These results indicate that the proposed approximation can serve as an efficient computational component for scalable Signed Particle Formulation based quantum simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an analytical approximation for the Wigner kernel in one-dimensional quantum systems, enhancing computational efficiency in phase space simulations.
AI.motivation: The aim is to address the computational challenges posed by the evaluation of the Wigner kernel in the Signed Particle Formulation framework, particularly when faced with oscillatory integrals in time-dependent simulations.
AI.method: The study develops a series-based representation of the potential function to create an analytical approximation of the Wigner kernel and associated Gamma function.
AI.result: The proposed method was validated against Gaussian-based potential profiles, demonstrating that it accurately approximates Wigner kernels and Gamma functions while reducing computational costs.
AI.conclusion: The new analytical approximation significantly enhances scalability and efficiency in quantum simulations using the Signed Particle Formulation.

title: Composing Quantum Instruments
comment: Independent work "The quantum instrument monad" by Tobias Fritz develops a closely related construction in the Schrödinger picture. The two works provide complementary Schrödinger- and Heisenberg-picture formulations
summary: We study the composition of classically-controlled quantum instruments--the natural quantum analogue of Markov kernels. Classically, Markov kernels compose by integrating one kernel against another. Defining this composition for quantum instruments with continuous outcomes requires an integral of quantum channel-valued functions with respect to a quantum instrument. We construct this integral in the Heisenberg picture using the Okamura-Ozawa normal extension to a von Neumann tensor product. This integral recovers the expected finite formula, preserves normal complete positivity and subunitality, and provides the multiplication for a monad governing the composition of quantum instruments. As an immediate consequence, we identify the category of quantum Markov kernels as the Kleisli category of this monad.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a framework for composing quantum instruments analogous to Markov kernels through an integral formulation, maintaining essential properties like complete positivity.
AI.motivation: The study aims to extend classical Markov kernel composition to quantum settings, addressing the complexities of continuous outcomes in quantum instruments.
AI.method: The composition is defined using an integral of quantum channel-valued functions, implemented in the Heisenberg picture via the Okamura-Ozawa normal extension within a von Neumann tensor product framework.
AI.result: The proposed integral formulation retrieves a finite composition formula and preserves key properties such as normal complete positivity and subunitality, establishing a monad for quantum instruments.
AI.conclusion: The findings classify the category of quantum Markov kernels as the Kleisli category corresponding to the introduced monad, linking classical and quantum frameworks.

title: Diameter truncated operator evolution
summary: We present a method for simulating operator dynamics in out-of-equilibrium quantum systems. Due to the rapid growth of complexity in these systems, this is typically speaking an intractable task. However, exceptional progress has been made in recent years to sidestep this barrier, with the introduction of a number of methods that make use of a truncation of the simulation to low-weight (the number of non-trivial terms in a Pauli string basis expansion) observables, which turns out to be a good approximation for many dynamical quantities of interest, e.g., two-point infinite-temperature correlation functions between local operators. In this work, we extend this idea to a leaner truncation protocol, truncating operators based on their diameter - that is, the size of the region on the lattice on which they are non-trivially supported. Using existing analysis for generic circuits we argue that this kind of truncation protocol is physically well-motivated, and show via extensive numerical simulations for a number of systems of interest (here, the kicked Ising model and the Heisenberg XXZ model) that it is effective, and allows us to efficiently and accurately extract local correlation functions and transport properties.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new truncation method for simulating operator dynamics in out-of-equilibrium quantum systems, focusing on diameter-based truncation to improve efficiency and accuracy in computing local correlation functions.
AI.motivation: The complexity involved in simulating out-of-equilibrium quantum systems has hindered progress, necessitating more efficient methods to approximate relevant physical quantities.
AI.method: The authors propose a truncation protocol that prioritizes operators based on their diameter, allowing for a more efficient simplification while preserving crucial dynamical information.
AI.result: Through numerical simulations of the kicked Ising model and the Heisenberg XXZ model, the authors demonstrate that this diameter-based truncation effectively captures local correlation functions and transport properties with high accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed truncation method offers a physically justified approach to simplifying simulations in complex quantum systems, enhancing both efficiency and accuracy.
